newsitem.title: CHINA: China searching for answers to pension troubles. [CORRECTED 16:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: China searching for answers to pension troubles. [CORRECTED 16:25 GMT]

text.p: China is considering deep changes to its social security system as its rapidly ageing population pushes a creaking pension programme towards bankruptcy, analysts said on Tuesday.
"China faces the most profound crisis in providing social security of any country in the world," said Michael Tanner, a pensions policy analyst with the U.S.-based Cato Institute, in an interview.

Pension plans -- largely unavailable to the villagers who made up about three-fourths of China's 1.2 billion population -- mainly relied on a "pay-as-you-go" scheme that pooled payments to support today's retirees, Tanner said.

That system would start running a deficit as the ratio of workers to pensioners fell in line with rising health standards and Beijing's family planning policy of limiting families to one child each, Tanner warned while on a visit to Shanghai.
China currently had about six workers supporting every pension-drawing retiree in 1997, and that would fall to about two workers per pensioner by 2030 (corrects year from 2015), he said.
"The pay-as-you-go system is going to fall apart in 15 to 20 years, so you've got to start phasing it out now," he said.

Urban pension reform was posing a problem for Beijing because most retirement plans were run by inefficient state-owned firms that had to provide cradle-to-grave support for workers, said Yu Mingde, an analyst with the China Centre for Economic Research.
Pension reform would further challenge communist China's traditional Marxist principles of communal welfare, already under attack from nearly two decades of capitalist-style economic reform, Yu said.
"We've had our experiment with egalitarianism and it didn't work," Yu said.
Chinese officials were looking with admiration on Chile's pension scheme, in which individuals put money into privately managed accounts, said Yu, who is involved in research in the area.

While China's fledgling financial sector was not developed enough to put pension money into the hands of private fund managers as in the Chilean system, Beijing would soon start experimenting with personal accounts, Yu said.
Yu said many villages had already started such plans, with an estimated 75 million farmers having saved about 10 billion yuan ($1.2 billion) in individual accounts.
"In many ways you can say they are more advanced than we are in the cities," Yu said.
Beijing was also studying the pension system in Singapore, where the government invested money from individual accounts on behalf of the workers, he said.

Pension money was now simply deposited in banks or put into government bonds, and while some free-wheeling areas -- such as Shanghai -- had illegally sunk funds into the stock markets in search of higher returns, real financial diversification would be some time away, Yu said.
China would probably adopt a two-tiered pension system that coupled the existing pay-as-you-go plan with a network of individual accounts that would pay out as much as was put into them, Yu said.
"This unified plan has not yet been made official in terms of a document," Yu said but declined to give further details.
